mcqs.question: Why can replicas drift out of sync even when every write successfully satisfies its quorum?
options: A quorum write only requires W out of N replicas to acknowledge, so it's normal for the remaining N-W replicas to miss the update if they were down or slow
Quorum writes are always applied to every replica simultaneously, so drift is actually impossible
Drift only happens when the wrong consistency model is chosen, never under quorum writes
It only happens due to a bug in the replication protocol
mcqs.explanation: A quorum write is designed to succeed once W of N replicas confirm it — the remaining N-W replicas can legitimately miss it if they were unavailable at that moment. This is expected behavior, not a bug or something a different consistency model would prevent by itself.

mcqs.question: What's the key limitation of read repair as a way to fix replica drift?
options: It requires taking the entire cluster offline while it runs
It can only repair one replica per day due to rate limiting
It needs a separate, dedicated infrastructure process to run at all
It only fixes a replica if that replica happens to be queried by a read, so cold, rarely-read data never gets repaired this way
mcqs.explanation: Read repair is opportunistic — it only touches replicas involved in an actual read, so data nobody reads never gets fixed by it. It requires no downtime, has no daily rate limit, and needs no dedicated infrastructure since it piggybacks on normal reads.

mcqs.question: Why do systems use Merkle trees instead of comparing every record between two replicas during anti-entropy?
options: Comparing every record directly is prohibitively expensive at scale; a Merkle tree lets replicas compare a single root hash first and only descend into subtrees whose hashes actually differ
Merkle trees are required by law for any replicated database
Comparing every record directly is actually faster, but Merkle trees are used for security reasons only
Merkle trees eliminate the need for anti-entropy to run at all
mcqs.explanation: The entire point of a Merkle tree here is efficiency: matching hashes let the comparison skip whole subtrees, avoiding a full record-by-record scan. There's no legal requirement, direct comparison isn't actually faster, and Merkle trees are the mechanism anti-entropy uses, not a replacement for it.

mcqs.question: A team disables background anti-entropy to save resources, relying only on read repair. What's the realistic consequence for rarely-accessed archived records?
options: No consequence — read repair alone guarantees full convergence over time
The records those replicas hold can remain permanently drifted, since nothing ever triggers a read-repair fix for data nobody reads
The database will automatically re-enable anti-entropy once drift is detected
Archived records are immune to drift because they're written only once
mcqs.explanation: Without anti-entropy, cold data has no mechanism forcing convergence — read repair simply never fires for records nobody queries, so drift can persist indefinitely. There's no automatic re-enabling, and being written once doesn't protect a record from an initial quorum write missing some replicas.

mcqs.question: A replica misses a delete, and anti-entropy doesn't repair it before the tombstone's garbage-collection window closes. What's the realistic consequence?
options: The deleted row can be resurrected, since the tombstone is gone and the replica's stale old value can look newer than nothing
Nothing — tombstones are permanent and never garbage collected
The cluster automatically extends the gc_grace_seconds window to compensate
The replica is automatically dropped from the cluster
mcqs.explanation: Once the tombstone is garbage collected, there's no longer a delete marker to reconcile against — a replica still holding the old value can look like the newer write, resurrecting deleted data. Tombstones are deliberately time-limited, not permanent, and neither auto-extension nor dropping the replica is what actually happens.
